Field studies on Black-tailed myiobius (Myiobius atricaudus) indicate that newly fertilised ova, resulting from a cloacal kiss, have an initial wet weight of approximately 1.74 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.74 grams], a value reflecting the modest energetic reserves provisioned prior to incubation. Clutches are consistently small; females lay exactly 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], with only a single clutch attempted each year [F_R_i = single clutch attempted each year], a reproductive strategy that appears constrained by the species' insectivorous diet and the high metabolic demands of nestling provisioning. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, an estimate derived from comparative data on the related eastern kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus), is approximately 4050 days [am = approximately 4050 days] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. However, under the thermal conditions that characterise its active metabolic periods, typically 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], individuals are estimated to attain a lifespan of around 11.1 years [am = around 11.1 years], a duration that places it among the longer-lived small passerines.

Incubation periods in this species are relatively extended for a tyrant flycatcher of its body size. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after 22 days [ab = 22 days], a developmental duration that likely reflects the energetic constraints associated with the relatively cool microclimate of the shaded, understory nests this bird favours. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately after hatching, averages 1.6 grams [Wwb = 1.6 grams], a value only slightly lower than the initial egg mass and indicative of minimal yolk conversion inefficiency during the incubation phase. Hatchlings are altricial and entirely dependent on parental provisioning, with the first feeding event occurring within hours of emergence from the calcareous shell. The nestling chick then enters a period of rapid growth, sustained by arthropod prey delivered at frequent intervals by both parents.

At the elevated body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which is typical of the species' active metabolic state, the developmental schedule proceeds in a predictable sequence. The time since birth at fledging, when the nestling first achieves sustained flight, is approximately 22 days after hatching [tx = approximately 22 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling period, consistent with values reported for other Myiobius species, is followed by a prolonged phase of parental care as the fledgling develops foraging competence. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 10 grams [Wwi = approximately 10 grams], a modest mass that reflects the bird's slender, active morphology adapted for sally-gleaning insects from the forest understory. Adults attain this asymptotic mass within several weeks of fledging, after which body mass remains relatively stable through the breeding season.

Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation and the capacity for gametogenesis, occurs at approximately 66 days after hatching [tp = approximately 66 days after hatching] under the standard thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity, compared to larger tyrannids, enables the species to begin breeding within its first year of life under favourable conditions. Field observations confirm that first-year birds frequently establish territories in the late dry season, though not all successfully secure a mate. The onset of reproductive activation is closely tied to photoperiod and prey abundance, with testosterone surges observed in males coinciding with the arrival of peak arthropod biomass. The gonadal swelling in both sexes is noticeable externally, and cloacal protuberance development in males proceeds rapidly following the initiation of territorial advertisement calls.

First reproduction, marked by the laying of the initial clutch, is typically deferred until one year after hatching [tR = one year after hatching] under the thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that prevail during the breeding season. This delay between sexual maturation and first successful breeding is common among small Neotropical passerines and is thought to reflect the time required for territory acquisition, pair formation, and the accumulation of sufficient body condition to support egg production. The conservative annual output of exactly 2 eggs per clutch and a single clutch per year reflects an adaptation to high nest predation rates and seasonal resource fluctuations characteristic of its humid lowland forest habitat. Post-breeding mortality increases sharply after the first reproductive season.
